Over the last few decades, laser wakefield accelerators (LWFAs) have grown from a theoretical concept [1] into a full, active research field, with applications relevant to high energy physics [2], medical diagnosis [3-6], cancer treatment [7-9], material research and inspection [10,11], and advanced light sources [12,13], among others. In LWFA, a high-intensity, ultrashort laser pulse interacts with an underdense plasma medium, driving plasma oscillations and creating an accelerating structure in its wake [14,15]; electrons placed in the correct location in the cavities, or bubbles, of this structure feel extremely strong forces accelerating them in the direction of propagation of the laser, as well as focusing them radially to the optical axis.
